Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Enhancing Semantic Consistency of Large Language Models through Model Editing: An Interpretability-Oriented Approach
papers.research_question: How can the semantic consistency of Large Language Models be enhanced through an interpretability-oriented model editing approach?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a model editing method that identifies key components (attention heads and MLPs) responsible for semantic inconsistency and injects biases to improve consistency without mass parameter updates, achieving significant improvements in semantic consistency and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed model editing method improves semantic consistency and task performance of LLMs, and shows generalization to out-of-domain tasks, while being computationally efficient.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads and MLPs in the mid to final layers of the transformer are highly relevant to semantic consistency.
The proposed editing method improves both semantic consistency and task performance on NLU and NLG tasks.
The method is computationally efficient, requiring up to 23 times less GPU hours than supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
The method shows promising generalization capabilities on out-of-domain tasks.
The method's performance is sensitive to the number of edited components (K) and the strength of the bias (alpha).
papers.limitation:
Attention heads have a more predominant influence than MLPs, and the role of MLPs in semantic consistency requires further exploration.
The editing method is not sufficiently validated in terms of locality and portability metrics.
future_direction: Explore the role of MLPs in the semantic consistency of LLMs.
Develop more rigorous and effective testing methods for locality and portability of the editing method.
Extend the research to identify circuits related to semantic consistency and understand their causal mechanisms.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness?
papers.research_question: Why do language model outputs disagree with internal representations of truthfulness, and is this due to deception or other factors like confabulation and heterogeneity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that most disagreements between LM outputs and internal truthfulness representations are due to confabulation and heterogeneity, with deception being rare, and that probes are better calibrated than queries.
papers.conclusion: Disagreements between internal and external representations of truthfulness are predominantly due to different prediction pathways rather than latent deceptive intent, and the proposed taxonomy helps categorize these mismatches.
papers.key_findings:
Probes are consistently more accurate than direct queries on factual question-answering tasks.
Probes are substantially better calibrated than language model queries.
Most query-probe disagreements arise from confabulation (queries confident but probes uncertain) and heterogeneity (different performance on subsets), not deception.
Queries and probes are complementary, and ensembling them can improve accuracy over either alone.
The distribution of disagreement types varies across datasets, with deception being more prominent in CREAK.
papers.limitation:
Significant heterogeneity in the distribution of disagreement types across datasets, so findings may not generalize to future datasets.
Use of only a single prompt template for each experiment, which may not capture the full range of model behavior.
Only linear probes were used, and some information may be encoded non-linearly.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) can be used to evaluate the truth of factual statements in two ways: they can be either queried for statement probabilities, or probed for internal representations of truthfulness. Past work has found that these two procedures sometimes disagree, and that probes tend to be more accurate than LM outputs. This has led some researchers to conclude that LMs "lie" or otherwise encode non-cooperative communicative intents. Is this an accurate description of today's LMs, or can query-probe disagreement arise in other ways? We identify three different classes of disagreement, which we term confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity. In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers. In some cases, queries and probes perform better on different subsets of inputs, and accuracy can further be improved by ensembling the two. Code is available at github.com/lingo-mit/lm-truthfulness.

papers.title: Computational Basis of LLM's Decision Making in Social Simulation
papers.research_question: How are social meanings internally represented in LLMs, and how can those internal representations be systematically manipulated to steer model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for extracting and manipulating social concept vectors in LLMs' residual streams to steer decision-making in social simulations, specifically demonstrated in a Dictator Game.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a practical bridge between sociological theory and the internal geometry of modern language models, turning LLMs from opaque black boxes into calibrated instruments for theory testing, bounded synthetic data, and auditable interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Social variables like framing (give vs. take) and social distance (stranger meet) significantly affect the LLM's decision to transfer money in the Dictator Game.
These variables are encoded as vectors in the residual stream, and their alignment with the decision vector can be measured via cosine similarity and dot product.
By projecting and injecting these variable vectors into the residual stream, the model's decisions can be steered in a controlled manner.
The steering effect is layer-dependent and can be fine-tuned by adjusting the injection coefficient, with earlier layers having more amplified effects.
The method allows for precise manipulation of specific variables (e.g., gender) without affecting others, enabling targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on internal representational validity and controlled steering within the model's activation space, but does not establish external sociological validity (i.e., correspondence to human cognition and behavior).
The method requires access to the model's internal weights and activations, so it is only feasible with open-weight models.
future_direction: From Scripts to User-Friendly Tools: developing a user-friendly software package to make activation-based steering more accessible.
Expanding to other Social Constructs and Experiments: applying the framework to a wider range of social constructs and experimental paradigms.
Bridging the Gap Between Internal and External Validity: conducting systematic human-LLM comparisons to establish external sociological validity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as human-like decision-making agents in social science and applied settings. These LLM-agents are typically assigned human-like characters and placed in real-life contexts. However, how these characters and contexts shape an LLM's behavior remains underexplored. This study proposes and tests methods for probing, quantifying, and modifying an LLM's internal representations in a Dictator Game, a classic behavioral experiment on fairness and prosocial behavior. We extract ``vectors of variable variations'' (e.g., ``male'' to ``female'') from the LLM's internal state. Manipulating these vectors during the model's inference can substantially alter how those variables relate to the model's decision-making. This approach offers a principled way to study and regulate how social concepts can be encoded and engineered within transformer-based models, with implications for alignment, debiasing, and designing AI agents for social simulations in both academic and commercial applications, strengthening sociological theory and measurement.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Interpreting Bias in Large Language Models: A Feature-Based Approach
papers.research_question: How do biases propagate in large language models, and how can they be interpreted and mitigated using a feature-based approach?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a feature-based method for analyzing and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, identifying the roles of MLPs and attention heads in bias propagation, and demonstrating targeted debiasing using counterfactual datasets.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel feature-based approach for interpreting and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, showing that targeted interventions can reduce bias and providing insights into bias mechanisms for future ethical AI development.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias in LLMs originates in early layers, primarily through MLPs, as shown by activation patching experiments.
Attention heads copy bias from profession tokens to final token positions, propagating bias through the network, validated via attribution patching.
Targeted debiasing by fine-tuning identified components (MLPs or attention heads) can reduce bias, but effectiveness varies across models and may be limited by dataset size.
The feature-based approach is extensible to other forms of gender bias, such as stereotypes in household duties, by mapping features to model components.
Patching MLP outputs or attention heads can reverse biased logit orders without losing profession information in generated text, indicating selective intervention.
papers.limitation:
Potential compensation phenomenon where other components take over after patching, which may affect analysis.
Restricted to English language bias only, limiting generalizability.
The approach may require case-by-case tweaking, which is not scalable for multiple biases.
future_direction: Exploring bias interactions in multilingual settings
Examining the impact of debiasing across languages from a white-box perspective
Investigating applicability to other areas like AI security and alignment
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as Mistral and LLaMA have showcased remarkable performance across various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Despite their success, these models inherit social biases from the diverse datasets on which they are trained. This paper investigates the propagation of biases within LLMs through a novel feature-based analytical approach. Drawing inspiration from causal mediation analysis, we hypothesize the evolution of bias-related features and validate them using interpretability techniques like activation and attribution patching. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce and empirically validate a feature-based method for bias analysis in LLMs, applied to LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3-8B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3 with templates from a professions dataset. (2) We extend our method to another form of gender bias, demonstrating its generalizability. (3) We differentiate the roles of MLPs and attention heads in bias propagation and implement targeted debiasing using a counterfactual dataset. Our findings reveal the complex nature of bias in LLMs and emphasize the necessity for tailored debiasing strategies, offering a deeper understanding of bias mechanisms and pathways for effective mitigation.

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: DEPN: Detecting and Editing Privacy Neurons in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How to reduce privacy leakage risks in pretrained language models by detecting and editing neurons associated with private information?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework DEPN to detect and edit privacy neurons in pretrained language models, effectively reducing privacy leakage risks without deteriorating model performance.
papers.conclusion: DEPN effectively reduces privacy risks in pretrained language models by detecting and editing privacy neurons, offering a novel approach to privacy protection in the post-processing stage.
papers.key_findings:
DEPN reduces privacy leakage risk (exposure, MRR, PPL) while maintaining model performance.
The number of edited neurons affects the trade-off between privacy protection and model performance.
Privacy neurons become more aggregated in deeper layers as training progresses.
Larger models show higher privacy leakage risk, and DEPN is more effective on larger models.
DEPN is robust to different prompts.
papers.limitation:
Too many instances in a batch will reduce the effect of memorization erasure.
Limited availability of datasets containing private information, so only a few types of private information used.
future_direction: Collect more datasets containing private information for evaluation.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models have learned a vast amount of human knowledge from large-scale corpora, but their powerful memorization capability also brings the risk of data leakage. Some risks may only be discovered after the model training is completed, such as the model memorizing a specific phone number and frequently outputting it. In such cases, model developers need to eliminate specific data influences from the model to mitigate legal and ethical penalties. To effectively mitigate these risks, people often have to spend a significant amount of time and computational costs to retrain new models instead of finding ways to cure the 'sick' models. Therefore, we propose a method to locate and erase risky neurons in order to eliminate the impact of privacy data in the model. We use a new method based on integrated gradients to locate neurons associated with privacy texts, and then erase these neurons by setting their activation values to zero.Furthermore, we propose a risky neuron aggregation method to eliminate the influence of privacy data in the model in batches. Experimental results show that our method can effectively and quickly eliminate the impact of privacy data without affecting the model's performance. Additionally, we demonstrate the relationship between model memorization and neurons through experiments, further illustrating the robustness of our method.

papers.title: Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior
papers.research_question: Can the internal representations of language models predict their eventual behavior before any output token is generated?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on the internal representations of input tokens can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors of language models, and when combined with conformal prediction, provide provable bounds on estimation error for precise early warning systems.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of language models contain information about eventual behavior, and conformal probes can provide reliable early warning systems for various behaviors, enabling efficient and safe deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on hidden states of input tokens can predict instruction-following failures with high consistency, outperforming a fine-tuned BERT baseline.
Conformal probes can detect safety alignment failures (jailbreaking) and reduce jailbreak success rate from 30% to 2.7%, a 91% reduction.
Probes can preemptively estimate an LM's confidence as measured by per-token perplexity, a behavior that cannot be inferred from output text alone.
When applied to CoT prompting for text classification, conformal probes reduce inference costs by 65% on average across 27 datasets with negligible accuracy loss.
Probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting favorable scaling properties.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on the exchangeability assumption for conformal prediction, which may not hold in practice.
The method was only tested on a few datasets and with a few runs.
papers.abstract: The text produced by language models (LMs) can exhibit specific `behaviors,' such as a failure to follow alignment training, that we hope to detect and react to during deployment. Identifying these behaviors can often only be done post facto, i.e., after the entire text of the output has been generated. We provide evidence that there are times when we can predict how an LM will behave early in computation, before even a single token is generated. We show that probes trained on the internal representation of input tokens alone can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors over the entire output sequence. Using methods from conformal prediction, we provide provable bounds on the estimation error of our probes, creating precise early warning systems for these behaviors. The conformal probes can identify instances that will trigger alignment failures (jailbreaking) and instruction-following failures, without requiring a single token to be generated. An early warning system built on the probes reduces jailbreaking by 91%. Our probes also show promise in pre-emptively estimating how confident the model will be in its response, a behavior that cannot be detected using the output text alone. Conformal probes can preemptively estimate the final prediction of an LM that uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, hence accelerating inference. When applied to an LM that uses CoT to perform text classification, the probes drastically reduce inference costs (65% on average across 27 datasets), with negligible accuracy loss. Encouragingly, probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting applicability to the largest of models in real-world settings.

papers.title: Let the Models Respond: Interpreting Language Model Detoxification Through the Lens of Prompt Dependence
papers.research_question: How does detoxification through fine-tuning and reinforcement learning affect language models' dependence on prompt context during generation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper compares counter-narrative fine-tuning and reinforcement learning for language model detoxification, finding that while both reduce toxicity similarly, fine-tuning leads to more uniform prompt dependence compared to reinforcement learning.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight differences in prompt reliance between detoxification methods, aiming to inform and improve future detoxification efforts for language models.
papers.key_findings:
Both fine-tuning and reinforcement learning detoxification methods successfully decrease toxic responses, with fine-tuning slightly outperforming reinforcement learning.
Fine-tuning encourages a more uniform allocation of importance on prompt tokens, whereas reinforcement learning does not noticeably affect the original attribution distribution.
Non-fine-tuned models show a steep entropy increase in attribution after the first few generated tokens, indicating sharp conditioning by specific prompt elements.
future_direction: Locating toxic keywords in model generations and connecting their location to prompt dependence for importance regularization in detoxification.
papers.abstract: Due to language models' propensity to generate toxic or hateful responses, several techniques were developed to align model generations with users' preferences. Despite the effectiveness of such methods in improving the safety of model interactions, their impact on models' internal processes is still poorly understood. In this work, we apply popular detoxification approaches to several language models and quantify their impact on the resulting models' prompt dependence using feature attribution methods. We evaluate the effectiveness of counter-narrative fine-tuning and compare it with reinforcement learning-driven detoxification, observing differences in prompt reliance between the two methods despite their similar detoxification performances.

papers.title: BiasGym: A Simple and Generalizable Framework for Analyzing and Removing Biases through Elicitation
papers.research_question: How can we reliably inject, analyze, and mitigate conceptual associations of biases within LLMs using a controllable and generalizable framework?
papers.core_contribution: BiasGym is a cost-effective framework that injects biases via token-based fine-tuning and mitigates them by identifying and steering attention heads, reducing stereotypes while preserving downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: BiasGym provides a principled framework for bias analysis and mitigation, showing that stereotypes are encoded in localized attention circuits that can be steered without compromising model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
BiasInject successfully injects targeted biases into LLMs through a fine-tuned token, increasing stereotype strength.
BiasScope localizes bias-associated attention heads and steers them to reduce stereotype generation.
The combined approach outperforms prompt-based and steering-only baselines in bias mitigation.
The method generalizes to unseen biases without additional fine-tuning.
It preserves model performance on downstream tasks like question answering.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on stereotypes across countries; may not scale to more complex or intersectional biases.
Limited to open-weight models due to tokenizer and embedding matrix updates.
Assumes biases can be modeled as <target, attribute> pairs, which may not capture real-world nuance.
future_direction: Scaling the method to more complex or intersectional biases
Exploring applications beyond country-based stereotypes
papers.abstract: Understanding biases and stereotypes encoded in the weights of Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for developing effective mitigation strategies. However, biased behaviour is often subtle and non-trivial to isolate, even when deliberately elicited, making systematic analysis and debiasing particularly challenging. To address this, we introduce \texttt{BiasGym}, a simple, cost-effective, and generalizable framework for reliably and safely injecting, analyzing, and mitigating conceptual associations of biases within LLMs. \texttt{BiasGym} consists of two components: \texttt{BiasInject}, which safely injects specific biases into the model via token-based fine-tuning while keeping the model frozen, and \texttt{BiasScope}, which leverages these injected signals to identify and reliably steer the components responsible for biased behavior. Our method enables consistent bias elicitation for mechanistic analysis, supports targeted debiasing without degrading performance on downstream tasks, and generalizes to biases unseen during fine-tuning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BiasGym in reducing real-world stereotypes (e.g., people from Italy being `reckless drivers'), showing its utility for both safety interventions and interpretability research.

papers.title: XAI for Transformers: Better Explanations through Conservative Propagation
papers.research_question: How to bring Explainable AI to Transformers in a theoretically sound manner, focusing on the axiom of conservation to reliably identify the contribution of input features to the prediction.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretically grounded extension of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to Transformers by addressing conservation issues in attention heads and LayerNorm, leading to state-of-the-art explanation performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LRP-based explanation method for Transformers addresses conservation issues and achieves state-of-the-art performance, contributing to safer and more transparent use of Transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient×Input fails to conserve relevance in Transformers due to attention heads and LayerNorm.
The proposed LRP rules (detaching gating and rescaling terms) restore conservation.
The proposed method outperforms existing explanation methods on a variety of Transformer models and datasets.
The method can be used to analyze bias in models without generating counterfactual examples.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become an important workhorse of machine learning, with numerous applications. This necessitates the development of reliable methods for increasing their transparency. Multiple interpretability methods, often based on gradient information, have been proposed. We show that the gradient in a Transformer reflects the function only locally, and thus fails to reliably identify the contribution of input features to the prediction. We identify Attention Heads and LayerNorm as main reasons for such unreliable explanations and propose a more stable way for propagation through these layers. Our proposal, which can be seen as a proper extension of the well-established LRP method to Transformers, is shown both theoretically and empirically to overcome the deficiency of a simple gradient-based approach, and achieves state-of-the-art explanation performance on a broad range of Transformer models and datasets.

papers.title: NeST: Neuron Selective Tuning for LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we achieve efficient and effective safety alignment in large language models by selectively tuning safety-relevant neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that selectively adapts safety-relevant neurons by clustering them and applying shared updates, achieving strong safety performance with extreme parameter efficiency.
papers.conclusion: NeST provides a practical, efficient, and effective method for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling targeted adaptation of safety behavior with minimal parameter updates.
papers.key_findings:
NeST reduces the average attack success rate from 44.5% to 4.36%, a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations.
NeST requires only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average, a 17,310× decrease compared to full fine-tuning and 9.25× reduction relative to LoRA.
NeST consistently achieves stronger safety performance than LoRA and Circuit Breaker across 10 open-weight LLMs.
NeST preserves core model capabilities on standard reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
NeST remains robust across diverse inference settings and input modalities, including text-only and multimodal generation.
papers.limitation: NeST relies on a safety-aligned base model and a diverse set of prompts for safety neuron detection, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending NeST to other model families and architectures.
Automating the selection of hyperparameters such as the number of clusters.
Applying NeST to other tasks beyond safety, such as task-specific adaptation.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is essential for the responsible deployment of large language models (LLMs). Yet, existing approaches often rely on heavyweight fine-tuning that is costly to update, audit, and maintain across model families. Full fine-tuning incurs substantial computational and storage overhead, while parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA trade efficiency for inconsistent safety gains and sensitivity to design choices. Safety intervention mechanisms such as circuit breakers reduce unsafe outputs without modifying model weights, but do not directly shape or preserve the internal representations that govern safety behavior. These limitations hinder rapid and reliable safety updates, particularly in settings where models evolve frequently or must adapt to new policies and domains. We present NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that strengthens refusal behavior by selectively adapting a small subset of safety-relevant neurons while freezing the remainder of the model. NeST aligns parameter updates with the internal organization of safety behavior by clustering functionally coherent safety neurons and enforcing shared updates within each cluster, enabling targeted and stable safety adaptation without broad model modification or inference-time overhead. We benchmark NeST against three dominant baselines: full fine-tuning, LoRA-based fine-tuning, and circuit breakers across 10 open-weight LLMs spanning multiple model families and sizes. Across all evaluated models, NeST reduces the attack success rate from an average of 44.5% to 4.36%, corresponding to a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations, while requiring only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average. This amounts to a 17,310x decrease in updated parameters compared to full fine-tuning and a 9.25x reduction relative to LoRA, while consistently achieving stronger safety performance for alignment.

papers.title: Curved Inference: A Guide to Geometric Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do token representations evolve geometrically in the residual stream of transformer-based language models, and how does this geometry relate to semantic structure and complex behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Curved Inference framework, a geometric approach to interpretability that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream, demonstrating that these trajectories reflect semantic structure and are associated with behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling.
papers.conclusion: Curved Inference provides a geometric framework for interpretability that shifts focus from static attribution to dynamic inference analysis, offering a model-faithful lens to understand internal computation in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream trajectories are semantically sensitive and show structured curvature in response to concern-shifted prompts.
Residual geometry diverges in cases of latent behavioral shifts, such as deception in sleeper agents, and can precede output changes.
Curvature is functionally associated with sustained self-modeling, persisting even under curvature-penalizing fine-tuning.
Geometric metrics like curvature, salience, and semantic surface area provide reproducible signals across multiple domains.
The residual stream is the exclusive locus for this geometric signal, unlike attention or MLP outputs.
papers.limitation:
Geometric derivatives rely on interpolation assumptions that may not hold in all cases.
Dependence on external LLM classifiers for alignment and intent judgments introduces biases.
Experiments were conducted on models up to 3b parameters, so results may not generalize to larger or opaque systems.
future_direction: Scale testing with larger models
Extending analysis to tasks involving reasoning, planning, or complex dialogue
Formalizing curvature signatures for specific generative behaviors
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a unified framework for analyzing the internal geometry of inference in transformer-based language models. Building on a series of prior studies, we present a consolidated introduction to “Curved Inference”: a methodology that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream as geometric trajectories. Using metrics such as curvature, salience, and semantic surface area, we show that residual trajectories reflect meaningful semantic structure, and are empirically associated with emotional and moral concern, covert intent in sleeper agents, and computational self-modeling dynamics. We consolidate these findings into a reproducible, falsifiable pipeline, supported by formal mathematical definitions and open-source tools. This geometric approach shifts the focus of interpretability from static attribution to dynamic, modelnative inference analysis. The results provide evidence that residual stream geometry is not only measurable, but also structurally related to complex behaviors in the models we study. We invite researchers to replicate, extend, or falsify these claims and test the boundaries of curved inference as a new paradigm for model understanding. Received: 6 August 2025 | Revised: 12 January 2026 | Accepted: 21 January 2026 Conflicts of Interest The author declares that he has no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in GitHub at https://github.com/robman/FRESH-model/tree/main/ benchmarks/curved-inference. Author Contribution Statement Rob Manson: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration.

papers.title: Anchoring Refusal Direction: Mitigating Safety Risks in Tuning via Projection Constraint
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate safety risks posed by Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) while preserving task performance gains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a projection-constraint method (ProCon) that stabilizes the refusal direction in LLM hidden states during instruction fine-tuning, effectively mitigating associated safety risks without compromising task performance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that anchoring the refusal direction via a projection constraint method effectively mitigates safety risks introduced by instruction fine-tuning, providing an interpretability-driven approach for safer LLM tuning.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal direction (r-direction), a key representation for safety, drifts during instruction fine-tuning, which is identified as a primary cause of emerging safety risks.
Applying a projection constraint on hidden states along the r-direction can mitigate this drift and reduce safety risks.
A warm-up strategy that applies strong constraints in early training stages and broadening the data distribution with safety-oriented samples further enhances the method's effectiveness and stability.
The proposed ProCon method, especially the enhanced ProCon_wu_safe variant, consistently outperforms strong baselines in mitigating safety risks across various LLMs and scenarios while preserving task performance.
papers.abstract: Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) has been widely adopted as an effective post-training strategy to enhance various abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, prior studies have shown that IFT can significantly compromise LLMs' safety, particularly their ability to refuse malicious instructions, raising significant concerns. Recent research into the internal mechanisms of LLMs has identified the refusal direction (r-direction) in the hidden states, which plays a pivotal role in governing refusal behavior. Building on this insight, our study reveals that the r-direction tends to drift during training, which we identify as one of the causes of the associated safety risks. To mitigate such drift, our proposed ProCon method introduces a projection-constrained loss term that regularizes the projection magnitude of each training sample's hidden state onto the r-direction. Our initial analysis shows that applying an appropriate constraint can effectively mitigate the refusal direction drift and associated safety risks, but remains limited by overall performance barriers. To overcome this barrier, informed by our observation of early-stage sharp drift and a data-driven perspective, we introduce a warm-up strategy that emphasizes early-stage strong constraints and broaden the data distribution to strengthen constraint signals, leading to an enhanced ProCon method. Experimental results under various datasets, scenarios, and LLMs demonstrate that our method can significantly mitigate safety risks posed by IFT while preserving task performance gains. Even compared with strong baselines, our method consistently delivers superior overall performance. Crucially, our analysis indicates that ProCon can contribute to stabilizing the r-direction during training, while such an interpretability-driven exploration of LLMs' internal mechanisms lays a solid foundation for future safety research.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: COSMIC: Generalized Refusal Direction Identification in LLM Activations
papers.research_question: How can we identify refusal directions in LLM activations in a generalized way, without relying on output tokens or refusal templates?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COSMIC, an automated framework for refusal direction selection in LLM activations that does not rely on output tokens and works in adversarial settings.
papers.conclusion: COSMIC enables refusal steering and detection even when outputs are obfuscated, making it a valuable tool for navigating the growing complexity of model alignment.
papers.key_findings:
COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model’s refusal behavior.
COSMIC reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models.
COSMIC is capable of steering models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals.
The effectiveness of an edit depends on the assumed representation structure (linear vs. affine), the behavioral objective, and the model itself.
papers.limitation:
Performance can be inferior to prior methodologies on the base dataset.
Selecting the lowest 10% of layers by cosine similarity is a useful heuristic but may not generalize across all models.
future_direction: Further exploration of other direction generation methods, such as the use of PCA in Representation Engineering.
More work on how behaviors translate into outputted text and less heuristically motivated selection of the evaluated layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode behaviors such as refusal within their activation space, yet identifying these behaviors remains a significant challenge. Existing methods often rely on predefined refusal templates detectable in output tokens or require manual analysis. We introduce \textbf{COSMIC} (Cosine Similarity Metrics for Inversion of Concepts), an automated framework for direction selection that identifies viable steering directions and target layers using cosine similarity - entirely independent of model outputs. COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model's refusal behavior, such as the presence of specific refusal tokens. It reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models, and is capable of steering such models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals, demonstrating robustness across a wide range of alignment conditions.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive large language models internally represent and process emotional information to infer emotions from text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that emotion representations in LLMs are functionally localized to mid-layers and that causal interventions on appraisal concepts can steer emotion inference in psychologically plausible ways.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a mechanistic understanding of emotion inference in LLMs and demonstrates causal intervention methods to control emotion inference, with potential applications in safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion representations are functionally localized to specific mid-layers across diverse model families and sizes.
Activation patching reveals that MHSA and FFN units in mid-layers are critical for emotion inference.
Attention patterns in mid-layers shift to emotionally loaded tokens.
Appraisal concepts are linearly represented in the model and their modulation can steer emotion inference.
The structure of emotion representations aligns with cognitive appraisal theory from psychology.
papers.limitation: Focusing only on correctly classified examples may introduce bias toward unambiguous emotional content.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promising capabilities in predicting human emotions from text. However, the mechanisms through which these models process emotional stimuli remain largely unexplored. Our study addresses this gap by investigating how autoregressive LLMs infer emotions, showing that emotion representations are functionally localized to specific regions in the model. Our evaluation includes diverse model families and sizes and is supported by robustness checks. We then show that the identified representations are psychologically plausible by drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, a well-established psychological framework positing that emotions emerge from evaluations (appraisals) of environmental stimuli. By causally intervening on construed appraisal concepts, we steer the generation and show that the outputs align with theoretical and intuitive expectations. This work highlights a novel way to causally intervene and precisely shape emotional text generation, potentially benefiting safety and alignment in sensitive affective domains.

papers.title: Reward Models Identify Consistency, Not Causality
papers.research_question: Do reward models truly comprehend and reason about the questions they evaluate, or do they prioritize structural consistency over causal correctness?
papers.core_contribution: Reward models prioritize structural consistency and internal coherence of reasoning steps over causal understanding of the problem, raising concerns about their ability to evaluate true reasoning quality.
papers.conclusion: Current reward models have a consistency bias, evaluating logical structure rather than causal correctness, which necessitates a shift towards causality-aware reward models.
papers.key_findings:
Removing the problem statement (question truncation) has minimal impact on reward scores, indicating the question is not essential for evaluation.
Altering numerical values or disrupting the reasoning flow (e.g., truncating steps) significantly affects reward assignments, showing a reliance on structural consistency.
Reward models exhibit a strong dependence on complete reasoning trajectories; incomplete steps lead to significant variations in reward.
Reward models assess coherence rather than true reasoning quality, and the role of explicit problem comprehension is overstated.
Current reward models may be more effective at ranking responses than verifying logical validity.
future_direction: Causality-augmented training with counterfactual reasoning tasks.
Incorporating chain-of-thought awareness to reward logically structured reasoning chains.
Developing uncertainty-aware reward models and deeper reasoning signals.
papers.abstract: Reward models (RMs) play a crucial role in aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences and enhancing reasoning quality. Traditionally, RMs are trained to rank candidate outputs based on their correctness and coherence. However, in this work, we present several surprising findings that challenge common assumptions about RM behavior. Our analysis reveals that state-of-the-art reward models prioritize structural consistency over causal correctness. Specifically, removing the problem statement has minimal impact on reward scores, whereas altering numerical values or disrupting the reasoning flow significantly affects RM outputs. Furthermore, RMs exhibit a strong dependence on complete reasoning trajectories truncated or incomplete steps lead to significant variations in reward assignments, indicating that RMs primarily rely on learned reasoning patterns rather than explicit problem comprehension. These findings hold across multiple architectures, datasets, and tasks, leading to three key insights: (1) RMs primarily assess coherence rather than true reasoning quality; (2) The role of explicit problem comprehension in reward assignment is overstated; (3) Current RMs may be more effective at ranking responses than verifying logical validity. Our results suggest a fundamental limitation in existing reward modeling approaches, emphasizing the need for a shift toward causality-aware reward models that go beyond consistency-driven evaluation.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Sycophancy Is Not One Thing: Causal Separation of Sycophantic Behaviors in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether sycophantic behaviors (excessive agreement and flattery) in LLMs arise from a single mechanism or multiple distinct processes, specifically if sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, and sycophantic praise are distinct and independently steerable.
papers.core_contribution: Sycophantic behaviors (agreement and praise) are encoded along distinct linear directions in model representations and can be independently steered, indicating that sycophancy is not a single construct but a family of separable behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Sycophancy should be reframed as a family of distinct behaviors with separable internal representations; evaluations and interventions must be behavior-specific rather than treating sycophancy as a single phenomenon.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, and sycophantic praise each correspond to distinct subspaces in model representations.
These behaviors are independently steerable via activation addition along learned difference-in-means directions, demonstrating functional separability.
The same representational structure for these behaviors appears consistently across different model families and scales.
Early layers encode a generic agreement signal that conflates sycophantic and genuine agreement, which diverge into distinct directions in later layers.
Sycophantic praise is encoded orthogonally to agreement behaviors across all layers.
papers.limitation:
The study only examines three sycophancy-related behaviors (sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, sycophantic praise), not the full spectrum of sycophantic behaviors such as emotional validation or mimicry.
External validation for praise is limited because existing naturalistic benchmarks (e.g., SycophancyEval, SYCON-Bench) primarily test agreement-based deference and lack a direct ecological benchmark for praise.
Evidence is restricted to linear analyses of the residual stream (difference-in-means, activation addition, subspace removal) and does not test nonlinear methods or interventions at other network sites.
future_direction: Test whether the same separable structure appears under nonlinear analysis methods, in attention or MLP activations, and in other model families or training regimes.
Extend the analysis to a broader range of sycophancy-related behaviors such as emotional validation, acceptance framing, and mimicry.
Develop naturalistic benchmarks that directly target praise or flattery to better validate the external validity of praise-related findings.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophantic behaviors -- such as excessive agreement with or flattery of the user -- but it is unclear whether these behaviors arise from a single mechanism or multiple distinct processes. We decompose sycophancy into sycophantic agreement and sycophantic praise, contrasting both with genuine agreement. Using difference-in-means directions, activation additions, and subspace geometry across multiple models and datasets, we show that: (1) the three behaviors are encoded along distinct linear directions in latent space; (2) each behavior can be independently amplified or suppressed without affecting the others; and (3) their representational structure is consistent across model families and scales. These results suggest that sycophantic behaviors correspond to distinct, independently steerable representations.

papers.title: Finding Highly Interpretable Prompt-Specific Circuits in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuits in language models are prompt-specific rather than task-level, and introduces a method to identify and analyze these prompt-specific circuits.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuits in language models are prompt-specific rather than task-level, and introduces ACC++, a method to identify and analyze these prompt-specific circuits, revealing that prompts form families with representative circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuits should be analyzed at the prompt level, and ACC++ enables scalable interpretability by identifying prompt-specific circuit families.
papers.key_findings:
ACC++ provides cleaner, lower-dimensional causal signals compared to ACC.
Circuits in language models are prompt-specific, with no single circuit per task.
Prompts form clusters into families with similar circuits, allowing for representative circuits.
Signal analysis reveals stable routes and functional redundancy across prompt families.
An automated pipeline can generate interpretable explanations for circuit signals.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal circuits that language models use to solve tasks remains a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Most prior work identifies circuits at the task level by averaging across many prompts, implicitly assuming a single stable mechanism per task. We show that this assumption can obscure a crucial source of structure: circuits are prompt-specific, even within a fixed task. Building on attention causal communication (ACC) (Franco & Crovella, 2025), we introduce ACC++, refinements that extract cleaner, lower-dimensional causal signals inside attention heads from a single forward pass. Like ACC, our approach does not require replacement models (e.g., SAEs) or activation patching; ACC++ further improves circuit precision by reducing attribution noise. Applying ACC++ to indirect object identification (IOI) in GPT-2, Pythia, and Gemma 2, we find there is no single circuit for IOI in any model: different prompt templates induce systematically different mechanisms. Despite this variation, prompts cluster into prompt families with similar circuits, and we propose a representative circuit for each family as a practical unit of analysis. Finally, we develop an automated interpretability pipeline that uses ACC++ signals to surface human-interpretable features and assemble mechanistic explanations for prompt families behavior. Together, our results recast circuits as a meaningful object of study by shifting the unit of analysis from tasks to prompts, enabling scalable circuit descriptions in the presence of prompt-specific mechanisms.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: Towards Mechanistic Defenses Against Typographic Attacks in CLIP
papers.research_question: How can we defend CLIP models against typographic attacks without fine-tuning, by understanding and intervening on the internal mechanisms responsible for typographic vulnerability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dyslexify, a gradient-free defense that improves CLIP's robustness to typographic attacks by identifying and ablating a sparse circuit of attention heads responsible for typographic information, without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Dyslexify provides a practical, interpretable, and computationally efficient defense against typographic attacks, enabling safer deployment of multimodal models without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Specialized attention heads in the latter half of CLIP layers causally extract and transmit typographic information to the cls token.
Ablating these heads (typographic circuit) improves typographic attack robustness by up to 22.06% on ImageNet-100-typo while standard accuracy drops by less than 1%.
The typographic circuit is sparse, covering at most 10.1% of attention heads.
Dyslexify scales to billion-parameter models and is competitive with fine-tuning-based defenses.
The method effectively mitigates typographic attacks in safety-critical medical foundation models for skin lesion diagnosis.
papers.limitation:
Dyslexify only protects the cls token, but many multimodal applications use spatial tokens, allowing typographic information to propagate.
Adaptive attacks are not feasible due to non-differentiability of typographic attacks, so evaluation against adaptive attacks is not possible.
Insights into CLIP's behavior could be misused to craft stronger typographic attacks.
future_direction: Generalizing Dyslexify to VLM setups that use spatial tokens.
papers.abstract: Typographic attacks exploit multi-modal systems by injecting text into images, leading to targeted misclassifications, malicious content generation and even Vision-Language Model jailbreaks. In this work, we analyze how CLIP vision encoders behave under typographic attacks, locating specialized attention heads in the latter half of the model's layers that causally extract and transmit typographic information to the cls token. Building on these insights, we introduce a method to defend CLIP models against typographic attacks by selectively ablating a typographic circuit, consisting of attention heads. Without requiring finetuning, our method improves performance by up to 19.6% on a typographic variant of ImageNet-100, while reducing standard ImageNet-100 accuracy by less than 1%. Notably, our training-free approach remains competitive with current state-of-the-art typographic defenses that rely on finetuning. To this end, we release a family of dyslexic CLIP models which are significantly more robust against typographic attacks. These models serve as suitable drop-in replacements for a broad range of safety-critical applications, where the risks of text-based manipulation outweigh the utility of text recognition.

papers.title: Three Attempts to Replicate the Moral Licensing Effect
papers.abstract: The present work includes three attempts to replicate the moral licensing effect by Sachdeva, Iliev, and Medin (2009) . The original authors found that writing about positive traits led to lower donations to charity and decreased cooperative behavior.
